original_text:
I have been reading about multi statement and multi table transactions. Currently delta only supports ACID at single table level and single transaction only. 

In order to handle multi table and multi transactions; There is going to be a shift from file system managed delta log(s3 or adls) to Catalog Managed logs in the future versions of delta lake. 

I think this is similar to how iceberg already operate ( not an expert in iceberg). In iceberg;catalog is already a final source of truth. 
 
As we all know Delta Lake stored all table metadata in the _delta_log directory:

1) Every commit is a JSON log entry.
2) When new parquet files are added; and 
once it logs the entry in transaction log; it consider it as a commit.

Here all powers reside within file system. What catalog can do is sync the metadata from transaction logs.

In the future versions of delta lake; we’ll see catalog getting more powers. Instead of the file system being the source of truth; catalog will have powers to accept or reject the transaction.

This is very helpful if multiple people are working on same table and they want to read their own versions of the data until you commit the transaction. 

Or if same person is working on multiple tables and wants to commit all the tables. Either the commits on the tables pass or all fail. In the current system, where delta logs are stored in S3, once the json entry for one table is logged, even if the other table fail, you can’t do anything about it and can’t rollback.

However, now catalog will decide whether the commit that was done in delta log; is it a valid commit or not. If it’s not valid ; it’ll just ignore that json file and vaccum will just delete that json log. 

If you are more interested to know about details; you can read more about how classic databases deal with repeatable reads, read your own writes etc.
…see more

ai_analysis.summary: The post describes Delta Lake's current file-system-managed transaction model: table metadata is stored in the _delta_log directory, commits are represented by JSON log entries, and adding Parquet files followed by logging the entry constitutes a commit. It claims that Delta currently supports ACID behavior only at the single-table, single-transaction level. The author predicts that future Delta Lake versions will use catalog-managed logs so a catalog can validate and accept or reject transactions across multiple tables, supporting all-or-nothing commits and allowing readers to retain their own data versions until commit. This future behavior is compared with Iceberg's catalog-centered source of truth. The post also says rejected JSON logs may be ignored and deleted by vacuum, while repeatable reads and read-your-own-writes are referenced through classic databases without further explanation.

interview_questions.question: According to the post, how does Delta Lake represent and complete a table commit when metadata is managed by the file system?
interview_questions.answer:
Delta table metadata is stored in the _delta_log directory.
Each commit is represented by a JSON transaction-log entry.
New Parquet files are added before the corresponding log entry is written to complete the commit.

interview_questions.question: How would catalog-managed transaction logs change multi-table commit coordination compared with the file-system-managed model described in the post?
interview_questions.answer:
The catalog would become responsible for deciding whether a transaction is valid and committed.
Commits involving multiple tables could succeed or fail together rather than leaving a partial commit.
Readers could retain their own data versions until the coordinated transaction is committed.

interview_questions.question: What comparison does the post make between catalog-managed Delta Lake logs and Iceberg catalogs?
interview_questions.answer:
The post predicts that Delta Lake will give catalogs greater authority over transaction validation.
It tentatively compares that direction with Iceberg, where the catalog is described as the source of truth.
The comparison is presented as the author's expectation rather than a detailed technical analysis.
